solution: The two pens are drawn one after the other with replacement, so each outcome is an ordered pair of colours and \(S=\{RR,\ RG,\ RB,\ RP,\ GR,\ GG,\ GB,\ GP,\ BR,\ BG,\ BB,\ BP,\ PR,\ PG,\ PB,\ PP\}\), with \(n(S)=16\). A occurs when Red appears in at least one of the two places. \(A=\{RR,\ RG,\ RB,\ RP,\ GR,\ BR,\ PR\}\), \(n(A)=7\).
_note: The printed key lists A as {RR, GR, RB, RP, GR, BR, PR} - GR appears twice and RG is missing. The count (7) is right, so this is a typographical slip in the key; the correct set is given above.

solution: With \(S=\{RR,\ RG,\ RB,\ RP,\ GR,\ GG,\ GB,\ GP,\ BR,\ BG,\ BB,\ BP,\ PR,\ PG,\ PB,\ PP\}\), \(n(S)=16\). B occurs when the two pens are NOT of the same colour, so B is S with the four like pairs \(RR,\ GG,\ BB,\ PP\) removed. \(B=\{RG,\ RB,\ RP,\ GR,\ GB,\ GP,\ BR,\ BG,\ BP,\ PR,\ PG,\ PB\}\), \(n(B)=12\).
The urn holds \(5+3=8\) coins and 3 of them are drawn together, so order does not matter. \(n(S)={}^{8}C_{3}=\frac{8\times 7\times 6}{3\times 2\times 1}=56\).
There are 5 distinct letters and 5 distinct envelopes, and no envelope is empty, so exactly one letter goes into each envelope. That is an arrangement of 5 letters in 5 places. \(n(S)=5!=120\).
The 6 books are all different and every arrangement of them on the shelf is one outcome. \(n(S)=6!=720\).
3 tickets are drawn together from 20, so order does not matter. \(n(S)={}^{20}C_{3}=\frac{20\times 19\times 18}{3\times 2\times 1}=1140\).

A is the event that the sum is divisible by 3 or 4 and B is the event that the sum is 7. Since 7 is divisible by neither 3 nor 4, no outcome lies in both, so \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and A, B are mutually exclusive. But \(n(A\cup B)=20+6=26\ne 36=n(S)\), so \(A\cup B\ne S\). A and B are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive.

C is the event that the first die is odd and D that the first die is even. A number cannot be both odd and even, so \(C\cap D=\varnothing\) and C, D are mutually exclusive. Also \(n(C\cup D)=18+18=36=n(S)\), so \(C\cup D=S\). C and D are mutually exclusive as well as exhaustive.

The first card is replaced before the second is drawn, so each of the two draws has all 4 cards available and an outcome is an ordered pair. \(S=\{(5,5),(5,6),(5,7),(5,8),(6,5),(6,6),(6,7),(6,8),(7,5),(7,6),(7,7),(7,8),(8,5),(8,6),(8,7),(8,8)\}\), \(n(S)=4\times 4=16\).

Now the first card is not replaced, so the second draw has only the 3 remaining cards; the pairs with a repeated card drop out. \(S=\{(5,6),(5,7),(5,8),(6,5),(6,7),(6,8),(7,5),(7,6),(7,8),(8,5),(8,6),(8,7)\}\), \(n(S)=4\times 3=12\).
Here \(n(S)=36\). A sum of at least 8 means the sum is \(8,9,10,11\) or \(12\), and these occur in \(5+4+3+2+1=15\) ways. \(P=\frac{15}{36}=\frac{5}{12}\).
Here \(n(S)=36\). The multiples of 2 on a die are \(2,4,6\) (3 ways) and the multiples of 3 are \(3,6\) (2 ways), so the favourable outcomes number \(3\times 2=6\). \(P=\frac{6}{36}=\frac{1}{6}\).
Here \(n(S)=36\). A product of 12 arises from \(\{(2,6),\ (6,2),\ (3,4),\ (4,3)\}\), so there are 4 favourable outcomes. \(P=\frac{4}{36}=\frac{1}{9}\).

Two cards are drawn together, so \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{2}=\frac{52\times 51}{2}=1326\). A pack has 12 face cards and 4 aces, and one card is chosen from each group: \({}^{12}C_{1}\times {}^{4}C_{1}=12\times 4=48\). \(P=\frac{48}{1326}=\frac{8}{221}\).
Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{2}=\frac{52\times 51}{2}=1326\). There are 13 clubs and 13 diamonds, one card from each: \({}^{13}C_{1}\times {}^{13}C_{1}=169\). \(P=\frac{169}{1326}=\frac{13}{102}\).

Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{2}=\frac{52\times 51}{2}=1326\). A suit can be chosen in 4 ways and 2 of its 13 cards in \({}^{13}C_{2}=78\) ways, giving \(4\times 78=312\) favourable outcomes. \(P=\frac{312}{1326}=\frac{12}{51}=\frac{4}{17}\).
Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{2}=\frac{52\times 51}{2}=1326\). A pack has 26 red cards, and 2 of them can be chosen in \({}^{26}C_{2}=\frac{26\times 25}{2}=325\) ways. \(P=\frac{325}{1326}=\frac{25}{102}\).

Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{2}=\frac{52\times 51}{2}=1326\). There are 13 heart cards and \(52-13=39\) non-heart cards, one from each: \({}^{13}C_{1}\times {}^{39}C_{1}=507\). \(P=\frac{507}{1326}=\frac{13}{34}\).

Three cards are drawn together, so \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{3}=\frac{52\times 51\times 50}{3\times 2\times 1}=22100\). Two queens from 4 and one ace from 4: \({}^{4}C_{2}\times {}^{4}C_{1}=6\times 4=24\). \(P=\frac{24}{22100}=\frac{6}{5525}\).

Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{3}=\frac{52\times 51\times 50}{3\times 2\times 1}=22100\). It is easier to use the complement: no diamond means all 3 cards come from the 39 non-diamond cards, \({}^{39}C_{3}=9139\) ways. \(P(\text{at least one diamond})=1-\frac{9139}{22100}=1-\frac{703}{1700}=\frac{997}{1700}\).

Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{3}=\frac{52\times 51\times 50}{3\times 2\times 1}=22100\). A suit is chosen in 4 ways and 3 of its 13 cards in \({}^{13}C_{3}=286\) ways, giving \(4\times 286=1144\) favourable outcomes. \(P=\frac{1144}{22100}=\frac{22}{425}\).

Here \(n(S)={}^{52}C_{3}=\frac{52\times 51\times 50}{3\times 2\times 1}=22100\). One king, one queen and one jack can be chosen in \({}^{4}C_{1}\times {}^{4}C_{1}\times {}^{4}C_{1}=64\) ways. \(P=\frac{64}{22100}=\frac{16}{5525}\).
The bag holds \(10+4+6=20\) balls and one is drawn, so \(n(S)=20\). There are 10 red balls. \(P(\text{red})=\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2}\).
Here \(n(S)=20\). The blue and black balls together number \(4+6=10\). \(P(\text{blue or black})=\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2}\).
Here \(n(S)=20\) and there are 6 black balls, so \(P(\text{black})=\frac{6}{20}=\frac{3}{10}\). \(P(\text{not black})=1-\frac{3}{10}=\frac{7}{10}\).
One ticket is drawn from 75, so \(n(S)=75\). The multiples of 6 up to 75 are \(6,12,\ldots,72\), that is 12 numbers. \(P=\frac{12}{75}=\frac{4}{25}\).
Here \(n(S)=75\). The perfect squares up to 75 are \(1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64\), that is 8 numbers (the next one, \(81\), exceeds 75). \(P=\frac{8}{75}\).
Here \(n(S)=75\). A number divisible by both 3 and 5 is divisible by 15, and the multiples of 15 up to 75 are \(15,30,45,60,75\), that is 5 numbers. \(P=\frac{5}{75}=\frac{1}{15}\).

A leap year has 366 days, and \(366=52\times 7+2\). So it surely contains 52 Sundays, and the question is whether one of the 2 remaining consecutive days is a Sunday. These two days form the sample space \(S=\{\)Sun-Mon, Mon-Tue, Tue-Wed, Wed-Thu, Thu-Fri, Fri-Sat, Sat-Sun\(\}\), \(n(S)=7\). A Sunday occurs in 2 of these pairs, so \(n(A)=2\). \(P=\frac{2}{7}\).

The bag holds \(5+4=9\) balls. With replacement the bag is the same for both draws, so each draw gives a red ball with probability \(\frac{5}{9}\) and the draws are independent. \(P(\text{both red})=\frac{5}{9}\times\frac{5}{9}=\frac{25}{81}\).
Without replacement the two balls are effectively drawn together, so \(n(S)={}^{9}C_{2}=36\). Both red can happen in \({}^{5}C_{2}=10\) ways. \(P=\frac{10}{36}=\frac{5}{18}\).

3 bulbs are chosen from 10, so \(n(S)={}^{10}C_{3}=120\). The room stays dark only if none of the three bulbs glows, i.e. all 3 chosen bulbs are defective, which can happen in \({}^{6}C_{3}=20\) ways. \(P(\text{room is dark})=\frac{20}{120}=\frac{1}{6}\).

The room is lit when at least one of the 3 selected bulbs is good, which is the complement of the room being dark. From part (i), \(P(\text{dark})=\frac{1}{6}\). \(P(\text{room is lit})=1-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6}\).

MOTHER has 6 distinct letters, so \(n(S)=6!=720\). Treating the vowels O, E as a single unit gives 5 units to arrange in \(5!\) ways, and the two vowels can be interchanged within the unit in \(2!\) ways: \(5!\times 2!=240\). \(P=\frac{240}{720}=\frac{1}{3}\).
With \(n(S)=720\) and \(P(\text{vowels together})=\frac{1}{3}\) from part (i), the required event is its complement. \(P(\text{vowels never together})=1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\).
With \(n(S)=6!=720\), fix O in the first place and T in the last place. The remaining 4 letters M, H, E, R fill the 4 middle places in \(4!=24\) ways. \(P=\frac{24}{720}=\frac{1}{30}\).

With \(n(S)=6!=720\), the first place can be filled by a vowel (O or E) in 2 ways and the last place by a consonant (M, T, H, R) in 4 ways; the remaining 4 letters fill the middle places in \(4!=24\) ways. Favourable arrangements \(=2\times 4\times 24=192\). \(P=\frac{192}{720}=\frac{4}{15}\).

Each of the 4 letters can go into any one of the 4 boxes, so \(n(S)=4^{4}=256\). If every box is to contain exactly one letter, the 4 letters are matched one-to-one with the 4 boxes in \(4!=24\) ways. \(P=\frac{4!}{4^{4}}=\frac{24}{256}=\frac{3}{32}\).

The Vice Chancellor and the 15 professors, that is 16 persons, sit at a round table, so \(n(S)=(16-1)!=15!\). For the favourable case, seat the Vice Chancellor first; the two particular professors take the two seats beside him in \(2!\) ways and the remaining 13 professors fill the other 13 seats in \(13!\) ways. \(P=\frac{2!\times 13!}{15!}=\frac{2}{15\times 14}=\frac{1}{105}\).
The bag holds \(7+4=11\) balls and 3 are drawn, so \(n(S)={}^{11}C_{3}=165\). All three black can happen in \({}^{7}C_{3}=35\) ways. \(P=\frac{35}{165}=\frac{7}{33}\).
